events.description: Governor of California approved act by legislature authorizing attorney general to bring suit for Indians of California, contingent on congressional authority. Presented by Dan Williams, sponsored by Indians of California.
President approved act conferring jurisdiction on Court of Claims to hear California Indian claims based on 18 unratified treaties of 1851-52. Initiated and sponsored by Indians of California, Inc.

Indian delegates representing auxiliaries of Indians of California, Inc. concluded a week's convention; 22 persons met with attorney general of California in his office with attorneys and organization representatives.
Attorney general of California filed action in Court of Claims on behalf of the Indians (Case No. K-344). Filed 15 months after passage of enabling act.
Court of Claims recognized J. W. Henderson, J. E. Pemberton, and James M. Hanley as friends of the court in case of Indians of California against United States.

Department of Justice advised office of attorney general of California that accounting report, together with report of Secretary of Interior, would be filed after plaintiffs signified they had closed their evidence.

Attorney general of California learned case had been placed on calendar for showing as to why it should not be prosecuted more vigorously; court threatened order to show cause why case should not be dismissed for want of prosecution.
Calling of the California Indians case by Court of Claims; attorney general of California was not present; friends of the court advised court of ongoing conferences and pending amendments.
Friends of the court filed action for J. W. Henderson to be recognized as attorney of record, and filed proposed amendments to attorney general's original petition with clerk of the court.
Friends of the court presented arguments for recognition as attorneys of record; amended petition containing all previously proposed amendments filed by Attorney General Webb.

Court of Claims held it was without authority to recognize anyone other than attorney general as attorney of record due to special act of Congress naming attorney general. Court authorized attorney general to file amended petition.
Amended petition filed in Indians of California v. United States No. K-344, including all Indians of California as defined by the act.
Accounting Department found method to advance California Indians case from November 1932 to February 1932; estimated preparation would not take a full year due to specific appropriations involved.
Secretary of Interior wrote to U.S. Webb stating accounting matter was taken up February 13, 1932 and would be furnished about August 1933.
U.S. Webb wrote letter to official of State of California regarding progress of government accounting in California Indians case, referencing November 23, 1932 Secretary of Interior letter.
Friends of the court advised by Washington associates that since March 21, 1932 court decision there is no court record of correspondence or evidence of procedure in the California Indians case.
Indians of California, Inc. (Indian Board of Cooperation) began its work, initially officered entirely by prominent white citizens.
Indians of California, Inc. (Indian Board of Cooperation) was incorporated under laws of the State of California.
Jurisdictional bill for California Indians introduced by Congressman John E. Baker in 1920 and Senator James Phelan, initiated by executive representative of Indian Board of Cooperation.
Case of Ethan Anderson v. Shafter Matthews, county clerk of Lake County; court held Indians are natural-born citizens entitled to vote and all privileges accorded to other persons.
Case challenging constitutionality of state law excluding Indians from public schools; court held law unconstitutional and Indians had right to attend public schools.

Steve Super and Benjamin H. Wilder v. John R. Weeks, Henry C. Wallace, Hubert Work, Federal Power Commission, and Henry C. Wallace as Secretary of Agriculture; court held Indians should look to Congress for redress for wrongful appropriation of lands.
Jurisdictional bill passed unanimously by Senate but failed to be reached in House due to calendar congestion before adjournment.
Nine Indians and other persons from California sought favorable consideration of reintroduced bill but opposed by Secretary of Interior Albert B. Fall.
Court of Claims bill approved and passed by both Houses but received pocket veto.
Congresswoman Kahn introduced counter-proposal bill at behest of Commissioner of Indian Affairs to appropriate $49,500,000 outright for California Indians, creating conflicting proposals.

testimony.location: Office of Attorney General of California
testimony.subject: Role of attorneys in California Indians case
testimony.key_claims: Webb stated he was not familiar with the work involved and not prepared to choose attorneys; expected to employ an attorney to do hard labor; recommended against making chosen attorney a deputy; wanted attorneys to remain in private capacity working with their clients; stated he had known Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley for many years and congratulated Indians on their choice.
testimony.questioner: Indian delegates including 20 representatives, J. W. Henderson, J. B. Pemberton, James M. Hanley

testimony.hearing: Court of Claims hearing on attorney of record
testimony.subject: Authority of attorney general versus private attorneys in California Indians case
testimony.key_claims: Webb argued authority under which he proceeded was unusual; found nothing more applicable in cases and authorities than cases cited by counsel; felt it would be worthless to submit cases at all. Court authorized him to offer amendments; amended petition included all amendments previously proposed by friends of the court, including all Indians of California as claimants.

testimony.hearing: Conference with friends of the court regarding amendments
testimony.location: Office of Attorney General of California
testimony.subject: Proposed amendments to original petition, particularly inclusion of all Indians of California as claimants
testimony.key_claims: Webb declared he did not agree with amendment including all Indians of California 'at all, at all, at all'; stated there was nothing in the law or hearings to justify such assumption; opined act only authorized suit on behalf of Indians who negotiated treaties and their descendants. Friends of the court showed by hearings and the act itself that Webb's interpretation was in error; Webb did not admit or deny validity at conclusion.
testimony.questioner: Friends of the court (J. W. Henderson, J. E. Pemberton, James M. Hanley)

testimony.witness_title: Delegate, Indian Board of Cooperation; member of Requa Indian Auxiliary and board of directors
testimony.subject: Representation of California Indians in Court of Claims case; desire for private attorneys; criticism of Attorney General Webb
testimony.key_claims: Indians of California are organized into more than 100 auxiliaries; Indians desire to be represented by Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley; attorney general took 15 months to file original petition which was inadequate; Webb failed to make amendments for over 2 years after errors were pointed out; retainer of $20,000 is less than $1 each for Indians of California; Indians never desired Webb to act for them; Indians are citizens of California and United States and have right to make own contracts.

testimony.witness_title: Delegate, Indian Board of Cooperation; member of Friant Indian Auxiliary and board of directors
testimony.subject: Representation of California Indians in Court of Claims case; desire for private attorneys; criticism of Attorney General Webb
testimony.key_claims: Same as Peter Williams affidavit; co-deponent; Indians desire Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley as attorneys; Webb's petition was inadequate and he delayed amendments for over 2 years; undue delay cost Indians hundreds of thousands of dollars in lost interest; Indians lost confidence in Webb.

testimony.hearing: Conference with friends of the court
testimony.subject: Progress of government accounting for California Indians case
testimony.key_claims: Accounting Department was not responsible for long delay; during 15 months between May 18, 1928 and August 12, 1929, 13 other Indian cases were filed giving them preference; found method to advance California Indians case from November 1932 to February 1932; would not take a full year to prepare accounting as only specific appropriations involved.

testimony.hearing: Congressional committee hearing on jurisdictional bill
testimony.committee: House and Senate Committees on Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Proposed jurisdictional act for California Indians
testimony.key_claims: Indians of California have prima facie meritorious claim against the United States; the bill properly protects interests of Indians and Government; recommended favorable consideration by committees.
